summary: Describes a format for LDAP Uniform Resource Locators, so a directory server, a search or an entry can be referred to by a link. It replaces RFC 1959 and was replaced by RFCs 4510 and 4516.

plainLanguage.summary: It gives a directory entry its own link, like a web address, so you can point to it and share it.

questions: what is the default ldap port
what does the bindname extension do
subtitle: A link format that names an LDAP directory entry, or a whole search, the way a web address names a page.

tldr.problem: LDAP directory entries and searches had no standard way to be written down as a link that a person or program could pass around.
tldr.mechanism: An LDAP URL starts with ldap:// and packs a server, a base distinguished name, attributes, a scope, a filter and optional extensions into one string, separated by question marks.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2255 replaced RFC 1959 and updated the format for LDAP version 3. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 4510 and RFC 4516.

today: RFC 2255 is obsolete: it was replaced by RFC 4510 and RFC 4516, and it was itself updated by RFC 3377. It replaced RFC 1959.

sections.title: What an LDAP URL Is
sections.content:
LDAP is the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol. RFC 2255 describes a format for an LDAP URL. The URL describes an LDAP search operation that a client performs to retrieve information from an LDAP directory.

The document replaces RFC 1959. It updates the format for version 3 of LDAP, clarifies how LDAP URLs are resolved, and defines an extension mechanism so future documents can add features, for example access to new LDAPv3 extensions.

The IESG note at the top warns that update access to LDAPv3 needs secure authentication, which this document does not mandate. Implementors were discouraged from deploying update functionality until a standard for mandatory authentication was published.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a way to write down where a directory entry lives, and what to ask about it, as a single line of text.

sections.title: The URL Grammar
sections.content:
An LDAP URL begins with the prefix ldap, then ://, then an optional host and port. After a / comes the dn, followed by the attributes, the scope, the filter and the extensions, each introduced by a ?. Every part can be left out, but only from the right.

The default LDAP port is TCP port 389. If no host and port are given, the client must have some prior knowledge of an appropriate LDAP server to contact.

  • dn: the distinguished name of the base object of the search.
  • attributes: a comma-separated list of attributes to return. If omitted, all user attributes are requested.
  • scope: base, one or sub. If omitted, base is assumed.
  • filter: a search filter. If omitted, (objectClass=*) is assumed.

Any URL-illegal character (such as a space), any URL special character and the reserved character ? inside a dn, filter or other element MUST be escaped with the % method from RFC 1738. A comma inside an extension value MUST be escaped the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: The link is like an address with optional extras: which phone book, which person, which details you want, how widely to look, and any special conditions. Leave out the extras and the computer uses sensible defaults.

sections.title: Extensions and the Bindname Extension
sections.content:
The extensions part is a comma-separated list of type=value pairs, where the value may be omitted. An extension prefixed with ! (ASCII 33) is critical; one without it is non-critical.

  • If the client supports a critical extension, it MUST obey it. It SHOULD obey supported non-critical ones.
  • If the client does not support a critical extension, it MUST NOT process the URL. An unsupported non-critical extension MUST be ignored.

Extension types starting with X- or x- are reserved for bilateral agreements between the parties. Other types must be defined in this document or in other standards-track documents.

This document defines one extension, bindname. Its value is the distinguished name to authenticate as while resolving the URL, and it may be the empty string to request unauthenticated access. Clients MAY implement it. If it is critical, the client MUST authenticate with that name; if not, the client MAY.
sections.plainLanguage: Extensions are optional notes on the link. A note marked with an exclamation mark means 'you must follow this or do not open the link at all'. Unmarked notes can be skipped if you do not understand them.

sections.title: Resolving a URL
sections.content:
A client SHOULD resolve an LDAP URL in four steps. First it gets a connection to the server named in the URL, or to a server of its choice if none is named. It may open a new connection or reuse one, and the connection may provide confidentiality or integrity, for example using TLS.

Next it optionally authenticates. This is required only if the URL has a critical bindname extension with a non-empty value. Otherwise the client MAY bind using a name and method of its own choosing, including no authentication.

Then it performs the search described by the URL. Fields the URL does not specify, such as size limit, time limit and deref, MAY be set at the client's discretion. Finally the client MAY close the connection or keep it open.
sections.plainLanguage: To follow the link, your computer connects to the directory, maybe shows an ID, asks the question written in the link, and then either hangs up or stays on the line for next time.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives several worked URLs. ldap:///o=University%20of%20Michigan,c=US names an entry on a server of the client's choosing, and the same with ldap.itd.umich.edu after ldap:// names it on a particular server. Both mean a base object search with filter (objectclass=*) that requests all attributes.

Other examples show requesting only postalAddress, a subtree search on port 6666 for (cn=Babs%20Jensen), and a one-level search of all children of c=GB. One example escapes a literal ? as %3f, and another escapes the LDAP backslash as %5c.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show real-looking links, such as asking one university's directory for just its postal address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Clients may meet many servers through URLs, and URLs are likely to be processed automatically. So a client SHOULD have a user-configurable policy about which servers to connect to and with which security mechanisms, and SHOULD NOT make connections that break that policy.

Sending authentication information may violate privacy. Without a policy permitting it, a client should use an anonymous connection. Reusable passwords sent to a server may be abused by the server or by eavesdroppers, and should not be used unless policy explicitly permits.

An LDAP URL can describe an arbitrary search, so following one may cause unexpected results, such as retrieving large amounts of data or starting a long-lived search.
sections.plainLanguage: A link can make your computer ask a stranger's directory a big question, so your computer should follow your own rules about whom to talk to and what to reveal.

data.title: LDAP URL grammar
data.code:
ldapurl    = scheme "://" [hostport] ["/"
             [dn ["?" [attributes] ["?" [scope]
             ["?" [filter] ["?" extensions]]]]]]
scheme     = "ldap"
attributes = attrdesc *("," attrdesc)
scope      = "base" / "one" / "sub"
extensions = extension *("," extension)
extension  = ["!"] extype ["=" exvalue]

items.label: Base object
items.desc: Search only the named entry. This is the default.

items.label: One level
items.desc: Search the entries one level below the named entry.

items.label: Subtree
items.desc: Search the named entry and everything beneath it.
